claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: A policy should govern LLM use in contributions to rust-lang/rust only, excluding subtrees, submodules, dependencies and other repositories.
claims.quote: This document establishes a policy for how LLMs can be used when contributing to `rust-lang/rust`. Subtrees, submodules, and dependencies from crates.io are not in scope.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: rust-lang/rust is currently receiving a flood of low-effort PRs mostly written by LLMs.
claims.quote: `rust-lang/rust` is currently dealing with a deluge of low-effort "slop" PRs primarily authored by LLMs.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: Having some policy makes slop PRs easier to moderate than handling every case individually.
claims.quote: Having *a* policy makes these easier to moderate, without having to take every single instance on a case-by-case basis.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: The policy deliberately bans more than strictly needed, including some valid uses, so that it is easy to understand and moderate.
claims.quote: This bans some valid usages of LLMs. We intentionally err on the side of banning too much rather than too little in order to make the policy easy to understand and moderate.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: A project-wide policy is impractical because agreement is nearly impossible, and teams legitimately need different standards since the compiler needs more correctness than Clippy.
claims.quote: There are also reasons for teams to have different policies; for example, the standard for correctness is much higher within the compiler than within Clippy.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: Looser rules for project members than for newcomers would entrench power structures and feel unfriendly to new contributors.
claims.quote: However, it reinforces existing power structures, creates more of a gap between authors and reviewers, and feels "unfriendly" to new contributors.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: A lenient "responsible use" policy ignores the reputational harm of work that feels LLM-generated and makes moderation much harder.
claims.quote: but this neglects the reputational and social harm of work that "feels" LLM generated. It also makes our moderation policy *much* harder to understand

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: An experimental framing with a circuit breaker forces the project to revisit and update the policy as circumstances change.
claims.quote: By having a "forcing function", we ensure that we don't just forget about the policy, but update it over time as facts on the ground change.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: Dropping the threshold-of-originality exception would leave well-meaning contributors choosing between discarding work, rewriting it, or lying about LLM involvement.
claims.quote: It has the disadvantage that it becomes easy for people to intend to follow the policy, but be put in a position where their only choices are to either discard the PR altogether

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: A total LLM ban could not reach agreement and would likely drive many people out of the project.
claims.quote: We could have a more strict policy that bans LLMs altogether. It seems unlikely we will be able to agree on this, and we believe attempting it will cause many people to leave the project.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: Having no policy would raise distrust, make review assignment more random, and waste contributor and moderator time.
claims.quote: However, it greatly increases the baseline level of distrust within the project; makes review assignment even more of a dice roll than it is already

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: US lawyers have initially indicated that LLM output likely poses no copyright problem under US law.
claims.quote: We have gotten initial confirmation from US lawyers that LLM output likely doesn't cause issues under US law.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: Private feedback received since posting suggests there is no silent majority opposed to the policy, though the sample is not representative.
claims.quote: But I still find it quite convincing as an indication that there isn't some kind of "silent majority" who oppose the policy.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: Is the policy so restrictive that it is worse than having no policy at all?
claims.quote: Do you think this policy is so restrictive that it's *worse* than not having a policy at all?

claims.author: Diggsey
claims.claim: Would the policy force maintainers to reject a small, clearly beneficial change just because it is marked as AI-generated?
claims.quote: If someone opens a concise, easily reviewable change that's a clear positive improvement, but marks it as AI generated, does the policy compel maintainers to reject it?

claims.author: Diggsey
claims.claim: The policy should give maintainers flexibility and set contributor expectations rather than impose hard rules.
claims.quote: Shouldn't the policy focus on giving more flexibility to the maintainers while setting expectations for contributors?

claims.author: Diggsey
claims.claim: Hard-and-fast rules will cause fairness disputes when one AI-assisted PR is merged and another closed.
claims.quote: The way this policy is written at the moment seems like it will open a whole can of worms about fairness

claims.author: Diggsey
claims.claim: The project should set guidelines that, if followed, guarantee fair review, leaving maintainers free to handle anything below that bar.
claims.quote: The Rust project obviously wants to do a lot better than that, so should establish guidelines which (if followed) guarantees contributions some level of fair review.

claims.author: Diggsey
claims.claim: Treating an honestly disclosed AI-generated PR as an instant code-of-conduct violation is untenable.
claims.quote: It's clearly untenable to treat "opening a PR and truthfully reporting it as AI generated" as an instant CoC violation, since people make be making an honest mistake

claims.author: Diggsey
claims.claim: Responses to AI-assisted PRs should depend on the quality of the PR.
claims.quote: Wouldn't it make more sense to base the follow up action on the quality of the PR

claims.author: Diggsey
claims.claim: In professional practice, low-autonomy AI uses like autocomplete, refactoring, boilerplate and tests are largely solved, while end-to-end work is risky.
claims.quote: Roughly speaking I would say 1-4 is mostly "solved" by modern AI models.

claims.author: Diggsey
claims.claim: AI is poor at actual code review because models are too agreeable to trust.
claims.quote: Interestingly I think actual review with AI is really bad. It's decent at assisting review but the models are far too agreeable to trust its feedback.

claims.author: Diggsey
claims.claim: The line should be drawn by the AI's level of autonomy, which is detectable, rather than by creation versus review.
claims.quote: I would say the important thing is not whether the AI was "creating", but the level of autonomy it has. This is also the only thing that's detectable in a PR.

claims.author: nikomatsakis
claims.claim: The Leadership Council should set up a small group charged with creating a permanent policy.
claims.quote: The LC establishes a group of 3-5 people who are charged with creating a permanent policy.

claims.author: nikomatsakis
claims.claim: This policy should be interim, lasting only while that group makes progress and reverting if it disbands without a replacement.
claims.quote: If the group disbands without establishing a new policy, this interim policy is reverted, and we can discuss how to proceed.

claims.author: nikomatsakis
claims.claim: The policy is worse than no policy because it sets a precedent that harms potential contributors.
claims.quote: yeah, I do think this is worse than no policy at all, because it sets a precedent that I think will harm potential contributors

claims.author: nikomatsakis
claims.claim: Once a restrictive policy is in place, its supporters will have no incentive to compromise later.
claims.quote: In future conversations, there would be no real incentive for those who favor restrictive policies to come to some sort of compromise.

claims.author: nikomatsakis
claims.claim: The policy reflects a small group with strong opinions, which is not enough for an issue this important.
claims.quote: I feel this policy is the result of a small set of people with strong opinions (myself included) and I think this issue is too important to treat that way.

claims.author: rl2939
claims.claim: Having no policy would put Rust on a negative trajectory.
claims.quote: I think _not_ having a policy will send Rust into a overall negative trajectory.

claims.author: rl2939
claims.claim: Groups exist that maintain lists of software made without AI, including programming languages and compilers.
claims.quote: There are networks and organizations who are creating lists of software that are not being made with AI.

claims.author: rl2939
claims.claim: A policy banning AI would attract contributors who prefer a language built without AI.
claims.quote: Having a policy that bans AI will bring potential contributors into Rust because they will support a programming language that does not use AI.

claims.author: Turbo87
claims.claim: Banning LLMs would also drive away contributors who value moderate LLM use.
claims.quote: there are quite a few people that see the benefits of moderate LLM usage. if we ban LLM usage then that would "_drive away_ potential contributors" too.

claims.author: alice-i-cecile
claims.claim: Policy should not be decided based on outside groups that list projects to shame them, since the same logic could argue against inclusive policies.
claims.quote: I feel like making decisions on the basis of uninvolved people who create lists of people/projects to harass, shame and attack is bad actually

claims.author: lumi-me-not
claims.claim: The No-AI list promotes projects opposed to generative AI and is not a harassment tool.
claims.quote: the Starlight Network No-AI list is for promoting projects that have a stance against GenAI. It is not meant as a tool for harassment.

claims.author: lumi-me-not
claims.claim: The compromise is acceptable because the main concern is AI authoring contributions, not AI used for review or lookup.
claims.quote: I'm overall happy with this compromise, as I'm most concerned about GenAI being used to author contributions, not as much about it being used to review or look things up.

claims.author: jackh726
claims.claim: The policy should either spell out a precise set of cases where LLM use is allowed or carry a time limit or automatic revisit criterion.
claims.quote: This policy as a whole is fairly decent, but I do not want to both 1) not carve out a very precise set of constraints where LLM usage is allowed for rust-lang/rust contributions
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

claims.author: jackh726
claims.claim: A time limit or automatic trigger would ensure the policy is revisited if today's concerns do not materialize elsewhere in the project.
claims.quote: not add a time-limit (or some other "automatic" criteria) to this in order to ensure that we revisit if the concerns today actually play out in other parts of the Project.

claims.author: nikomatsakis
claims.claim: The rust-lang/rust policy is central enough to effectively commit the whole project, so the Leadership Council should decide it.
claims.quote: my personal opinion is that the policy on rust-lang/rust is central enough that this is effecively "committing the project" and should be a leadership council decision.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: The policy is not meant to commit the project or disrupt teams already using LLMs, and the council is not the right body because top-level teams decide their own purview.
claims.quote: I think it is very clearly *not* the intent of the RFC that established the leadership council to allow it to override the decisions of top-level teams.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: An alternative set of guidelines for allowing LLM-authored code has been drafted, adapted from earlier suggestions.
claims.quote: In https://github.com/jyn514/rust-forge/pull/1 I wrote up the guidelines I'd like to see if we allowed LLM-authored code
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: The FCP already includes most teams the council represents, and teams not on it are unaffected.
claims.quote: we already have a lot of the teams the leadership council is meant to represent on the FCP itself, and the teams that are absent are notably able to completely disregard these rules.

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: Because many teams touch rust-lang/rust, even a permissive org-wide policy would likely be stricter for this repo.
claims.quote: because so many teams touch this repo, it's highly likely that any permissive policy that applies to the whole org would be stricter in this case.

claims.author: Manishearth
claims.claim: The policy must explicitly allow clearly marked, vetted AI-generated reports on PRs and issues so security work is not impeded.
claims.quote: I think explicitly allowing clearly marked, vetted, AI-generated reports be attached to PRs/issues is something we will have to do in order to not impede security work.

claims.author: Manishearth
claims.claim: Clearly quoted and marked LLM reports are acceptable as supplemental material as long as the issue or PR stands on its own.
claims.quote: AI-generated reports are supplemental material, so that's fine. We still expect issues/PRs to be readable without needing to go through the report.

claims.author: Manishearth
claims.claim: If AI-found security issues flood in and libs needs LLMs to fix them, an exemption can be explicitly requested later.
claims.quote: if that's the case then that exemption can be explicitly requested (it would be a nontrivial conversation; LLM use to fix security issues is a complex topic).

claims.author: Kobzol
claims.claim: The policy is balanced: it allows LLM use in various ways and avoids taking a general stance on AI, so it does not read as pro- or anti-AI.
claims.quote: But this policy has been *very* carefully designed to allow LLM usage in various complicated ways, and to avoid making comments on the larger scope discussion topics about AI in general.

claims.author: Kobzol
claims.claim: Sending the policy to the Leadership Council undermines its purpose of being repo-scoped so it could land in reasonable time.
claims.quote: Going to LC subverts the original motivation of the policy, which was explicitly created to NOT be Project-wide, and to not have to go through the LC

claims.author: Kobzol
claims.claim: Escalating repo-specific policies into project-wide ones has repeatedly blocked previous LLM policies.
claims.quote: this is *exactly* the same filibuster that already stopped several previous policies in their tracks.

claims.author: Darksonn
claims.claim: Because it bans writing code, the most important LLM use case, the policy can reasonably be read as anti-AI.
claims.quote: The policy bans the number one most important use-case of LLMs in the programming space (writing code), so of course it can be seen as an anti-AI policy.

claims.author: Kobzol
claims.claim: The policy does not fully ban LLM-written code and is nuanced enough, with stated motivation, not to read as a project stance on AI.
claims.quote: The policy also does not actually completely ban writing code with LLMs either, in its current form.

claims.author: nikomatsakis
claims.claim: The teams that review rust-lang/rust are entitled to set its policy, even if that is not the best way to decide.
claims.quote: I agree it's within the rights of the teams that review code on rust-lang/rust to set the policy, what I wrote earlier was too strong in this respect.

claims.author: nikomatsakis
claims.claim: The better path would have been an LC-appointed group to gather data, deliberate and reach conclusions, possibly with a quick interim ban on slop.
claims.quote: I continue to think that the correct way forward would've been for the LC to set out a group of people to gather feedback, deliberate, gather data, and come to some conclusions

claims.author: nikomatsakis
claims.claim: Requiring a 40-checkbox multi-team FCP to change the policy will make future changes very hard.
claims.quote: If the precedent is that changing this policy requires getting 40 checkboxes, I think it's going to be very hard to make any changes.

claims.author: petrochenkov
claims.claim: A wide range of policies would be acceptable apart from extremes like mandatory slop review or a total ban.
claims.quote: I'd personally be fine with a wide range of policies, except perhaps most extreme ones like "you must review slop" or "no LLMs at all, even in you free time".

claims.author: petrochenkov
claims.claim: Handling LLM contributions case by case with reviewer judgement would also be fine, because there are not many of them in rust-lang/rust right now.
claims.quote: I'd also be fine with not having a policy and dealing with contributions involving LLMs on case by case basis, using reviewer's judgement

claims.author: petrochenkov
claims.claim: The number of LLM-involved contributions to rust-lang/rust is currently small.
claims.quote: the number of such contributions to rust-lang/rust is not actually large at the moment.

claims.author: Manishearth
claims.claim: Decisions this contentious are the kind the project should delegate to a small trusted top-level body for consensus-building and ratification.
claims.quote: I think this is exactly the type of tricky decision where the Rust project should _want_ to delegate consensusbuilding and final ratification to the toplevel team.

claims.author: nikomatsakis
claims.claim: Does the policy really disallow LLM-generated content outside specific cases even for experienced developers, who would have to go through the experimental process?
claims.quote: I'm actually not sure -- *is* this what the policy says? If you are an experienced dev, are we saying that in that case it's ok?
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

claims.author: teohhanhui
claims.claim: The policy is not neutral on moral, social and environmental issues, because merely having it sets a precedent.
claims.quote: The conclusion ("this policy is relevant regardless of the outcome of these discussions") seems unwarranted here. The mere presence of this policy will already be setting a great precedent.

claims.author: teohhanhui
claims.claim: Having no stated policy at all should be considered among the alternatives.
claims.quote: I ask that you consider the impact of having this policy document at all vs. not having it.

claims.author: AthenaEryma
claims.claim: A full ban is preferable because slower development beats the risks of LLM-generated code in a compiler valued for safety and reliability.
claims.quote: I would vastly prefer a slower pace of development than the risks inherent to language model generated code in the compiler I use explicitly for its safety and reliability.

claims.author: AthenaEryma
claims.claim: Ruling the main objections out of scope does not make them irrelevant; it just sets them aside to push a looser policy through.
claims.quote: Lack of ability to come to consensus does not mean these issues are not relevant to the policy

claims.author: ChayimFriedman2
claims.claim: Some people disagree with a full ban, and a community project can only pass policy by consensus among its members.
claims.quote: As a community-organized project the only way to pass a policy is to have consensus on it, and that consensus will come from project members, not from the outside.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: The people who wrote the policy also merge rustc code, so if they are trusted for safety and reliability they can be trusted to allow LLMs safely.
claims.quote: If you trust our judgement for creating a compiler that works safely and reliably, I ask you to also trust our judgement that we can allow LLMs in a way that doesn't affect that safety and reliability.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: Someone who certifies safety-critical rustc builds to TÜV believes the policy's rules will not hurt reliability.
claims.quote: I feel comfortable that the rules in our policy won't hurt the reliability of our or their software, and I sign my name to that fact every 3 months to TÜV.

claims.author: AthenaEryma
claims.claim: The process only appears to have consensus because it ruled one side's arguments off limits.
claims.quote: This is pretending at consensus by declaring half the points against one side off limits.

claims.author: AthenaEryma
claims.claim: Even limited permission for LLM-generated code is too much.
claims.quote: it still permits LLM-generated code. Under quite limited circumstances, yet still more than I am comfortable with

claims.author: AthenaEryma
claims.claim: Over the long term, humans cannot reliably manage output from machines designed to look good, because those machines erode users' skill and judgement.
claims.quote: I do not trust humans, long-term, to be able to manage the output of a machine specifically designed to produce good-looking output

claims.author: ismay-tue
claims.claim: Trusting the maintainers' judgement on code does not mean trusting their judgement on LLM policy.
claims.quote: If I trust your judgement on code, that does not imply I trust your judgement in other areas.

claims.author: jackh726
claims.claim: The added section on experimental LLM use resolves the concern even though there is no automatic expiry, and a better policy is unlikely soon.
claims.quote: The additional section on experimental LLM usage resolves my concern.
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

claims.author: jackh726
claims.claim: Bringing in the Leadership Council would add process without helping, since the policy is balanced across many stakeholders.
claims.quote: I also think this is well-balanced enough with enough stakeholders that introducing extra process to this (by bringing in the LC) isn't going to help anything.

claims.author: jackh726
claims.claim: The policy is long and hard to follow, but that reflects the nuance needed now; it can be summarized after merging.
claims.quote: I think it is a bit long, and can be hard to follow. I also think that's just the state of the conversation right now and nuance we have to draw.

claims.author: jackh726
claims.claim: Requiring authors to find a reviewer first is not an ideal intake path for LLM-generated code, but limited review capacity means no better option is available yet.
claims.quote: I personally would love for us to have a better intake system for LLM-generated code than "you need to find a reviewer first"
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

claims.author: jackh726
claims.claim: The no-soundness-critical-code condition is largely left to reviewer discretion, but the guidelines are good and discussing changes with the reviewer ahead of time helps.
claims.quote: I think the condition of "no soundness-critical code" *is* largely left to the discretion of the reviewer here - but I think the guidelines here are good.
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

claims.author: nikomatsakis
claims.claim: A strength of the policy is that it moves cautiously, leaving room for LLM-authored content while defaulting to no.
claims.quote: What I like about is it that it moves slowly and carefully, leaving room for LLM-authored content while making the default negative.
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

claims.author: nikomatsakis
claims.claim: The policy's complex lists of rules signal low trust in fellow reviewers.
claims.quote: However, I think what really bothers me about is that it signals such a low trust in our fellow reviewers.
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

claims.author: nikomatsakis
claims.claim: If some reviewers are allowed to review LLM-authored content, the policy should just permit that and rely on reviewers talking to each other about standards.
claims.quote: I think if we are going to allow some folks to review LLM-authored content, let's just do it, and assume that we can all talk to one another
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

claims.author: nikomatsakis
claims.claim: Instead of over-specifying review details, a group of people should experiment with the best way to handle LLM content.
claims.quote: I just think that there should be a group of people who are experimenting with the best option.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: Only a full ban would satisfy those with ethical concerns, and there is no consensus for one, so restating those concerns does not help.
claims.quote: We came to the conclusion that the people with ethical concerns will not be satisfied by anything less than a full ban, and we do not have a consensus to pass a full ban.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: Would opponents prefer no Rust project, or no policy at all, over one that uses LLMs?
claims.quote: Would you rather have *no* Rust project than a Rust project that uses LLMs? Would you rather have no policy at all?

claims.author: dballesg
claims.claim: Rust would be better off disappearing than allowing LLM code that will introduce many bugs, at odds with its goal of safety.
claims.quote: I would prefer Rust to dissapear if is going to allow non working and non functional code, that will plague it with thousands of bugs to be committed into it.

claims.author: dballesg
claims.claim: LLMs do not generate working code, so the only acceptable choice is a full ban.

claims.author: anotak
claims.claim: The social friction around LLMs, shown by the need for moderation rules, will cost the community more than LLM-authored code is worth, even with the policy's caveats.
claims.quote: I think that friction will be much more costly than the benefits of allowing LLM-authored code, even with the caveats in place in the current PR.

claims.author: anotak
claims.claim: Compiler-team decisions shape Rust's wider culture and should not be judged in isolation.
claims.quote: The decisions here have a top-down effect on the larger culture of Rust. They should not be viewed in isolation of just the language itself.

claims.author: ismay-tue
claims.claim: The decision process should include every aspect of the debate, including those ruled off topic, so everyone feels heard.
claims.quote: I would personally recommend to not shy away from including all aspects of this debate in your decision making process though.

claims.author: ismay-tue
claims.claim: If the process is causing conflict, people experienced in facilitating such processes should be brought in, since it is a social problem as well as an engineering one.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: Worldwide consensus is impossible, so project members decide while outside input is heard but not decisive.
claims.quote: We chose (we have chosen, we will continue to choose) people in the project as the ones who get a say.

claims.author: TheLastZombie
claims.claim: If a project can only survive by using an inherently harmful technology, it is worth asking whether it should continue at all.

claims.author: nnethercote
claims.claim: The project currently places almost no restrictions on LLM use, and this policy would add significant ones.

claims.author: nnethercote
claims.claim: Because members hold a wide range of views and decisions require consensus, the policy reflects what is politically possible.

claims.author: The-personified-devil

claims.author: reillypascal

claims.author: reillypascal

claims.author: Diggsey

claims.author: clarfonthey

claims.author: clarfonthey

claims.author: astrojuanlu

claims.author: astrojuanlu

claims.author: ChayimFriedman2

claims.author: cloudskater

claims.author: arirei

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: The policy should say explicitly that LLMs are an optional tool and never a requirement for contributing.
claims.quote: Note explicitly that LLMs should not become a *requirement* to contribute, that they should be at most an optional tool.

claims.author: BoxyUwU
claims.claim: Because the late changes were large, the FCP should get extra time so everyone can review them.
claims.quote: I think it's worth giving this a bit of additional time over the normal FCP period just to make sure everyone is aware and had the time to review those changes.

claims.author: BoxyUwU
claims.claim: The added rules will be very hard to change later, so the FCP should not be pushed through with the plan of fixing objections afterwards.
claims.quote: the process for changing the added rules in the future is really quite high so it feels somewhat important to me that we don't just bias towards the FCP passing

claims.author: tmandry
claims.claim: Halting merges of a whole category of PRs for ten days because an arbitrary limit was hit is an unjustified last-minute change.
claims.quote: Are we actually going to ban merging a category of PRs for _ten days_ because we hit an arbitrary limit?

claims.author: tmandry
claims.claim: The circuit breaker turns the policy's goal from reducing harm into enforcing an aesthetic limit on adoption.
claims.quote: This addition shifts the goal entirely to enforcing a kind of aesthetic limit.

claims.author: tmandry
claims.claim: The circuit breaker is excessive control and tells LLM-using contributors they are second-class and unwelcome.
claims.quote: sends a strong and clear signal to a class of contributors that they are second-class and not welcome here

claims.author: tmandry
claims.claim: A rule about meetings does not belong in a policy about accepting code to rust-lang/rust and would make it incoherent.
claims.quote: This is a policy about accepting code to rust-lang/rust. Under what logic does it extend to _meetings_?

claims.author: tmandry
claims.claim: Policies have to be legible to the people they cover, so meeting rules cannot be tucked into a PR policy.
claims.quote: To be effective, policies need to be _legible_ to the people they apply to.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: The meetings provision is out of scope and will be reverted.
claims.quote: I agree this is out of scope for the policy, I'll revert this.

claims.author: joshtriplett
claims.claim: The policy's LLM experiment previously had no parameters, success criteria or end, so it was a permanent arrangement rather than a real experiment.
claims.quote: The problem is that that experiment (previously) had no experimental parameters, no success or failure criteria, no end, and no motivation to establish further non-experimental policies for such contributions

claims.author: joshtriplett
claims.claim: Ending the experiment after a fixed time or a fixed number of PRs would not work, because no default outcome would get everyone to negotiate.
claims.quote: So, any kind of "after X time" or "after X PRs" would not work there.

claims.author: joshtriplett
claims.claim: If LLMs are used in more than half of PRs, the arrangement is no longer an experiment, which justifies the circuit breaker.
claims.quote: if *more than half of PRs to Rust* are using LLMs, *it's not an experiment anymore*, and a policy setting out to do an experiment is no longer appropriate.

claims.author: joshtriplett
claims.claim: One harm the policy has to prevent is pushing non-LLM contributors out of the project or making them second-class.
claims.quote: One of the important harmful effects to avoid is driving people who *don't* use LLMs out of the project, or making them second-class contributors.

claims.author: traviscross
claims.claim: Calling something experimental is a forward-looking label, and the project has to be ready for its provisions to become permanent.
claims.quote: like *interim*, *experimental* is forward looking.  We may not *intend* for some parts to be permanent, but we have to be *prepared* for the fact that they might be permanent

claims.author: traviscross
claims.claim: The policy will be hard to change, because any change needs nobody to raise a blocking concern.
claims.quote: Changing the policy later is going to require that nobody raises a blocking concern.

claims.author: traviscross
claims.claim: The 50% threshold with a default halt has the same problem: its default will not bring everyone back to negotiate.
claims.quote: the recent change to add a 50% threshold and set a default of halting work at that point creates the same problem described

claims.author: joshtriplett
claims.claim: If the experiment is treated as a real experiment, the circuit breaker sets a boundary no side wants, which forces a review of how it is going.
claims.quote: I think the circuit-breaker makes perfect sense as a way to set a boundary on that experiment that *isn't an ideal and desirable end state for any stakeholders*

claims.author: joshtriplett
claims.claim: Passing the policy while people disagree on whether the experiment is temporary or indefinite will cause trouble later.
claims.quote: If some people see the experiment as an experiment, and some people see it as a thing likely to continue indefinitely, that expectation mismatch is going to blow up in our faces later.

claims.author: traviscross
claims.claim: The compromise provisions will stay in force until changed, whatever experimental label some of them carry.
claims.quote: The normative provisions in this compromise policy will be the enduring ones until we change them, regardless of what purpose each of us sees in some provisions having been marked as experimental.

claims.author: traviscross
claims.claim: The 50% limit would not reliably bring both sides back to the table and could deepen polarization.
claims.quote: This limit would not necessarily bring all sides to the table and risks further polarization.

claims.author: traviscross
claims.claim: Reaching 50% approved AI-assisted PRs would look like success to some and alarm others, pushing the two sides further apart.
claims.quote: If we reach 50% of merged (and therefore *approved*) PRs being AI assisted, that'd sound like a successful experiment to me.

claims.author: traviscross
claims.claim: The LLM allowance cannot be time-limited without breaking the compromise, which shows it is more than a pure experiment.
claims.quote: the fact that we cannot time bound these without perturbing the compromise suggests, indeed, *something* is at stake beyond a pure experiment
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: The policy text says explicitly that the experiment exists to inform future policy and is not meant to be permanent.
claims.quote: This experiment is meant to inform future non-experimental policy, not to serve as the perpetual LLM usage policy.

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: The policy has no clause for ending the experiment, which leaves people unsure how to regard it.
claims.quote: an experiment can always be terminated, but such clause does not exist in the policy and thus people feel conflicted on how to feel about that.

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: This should be an interim policy, later replaced by a project-wide policy adopted through an RFC.
claims.quote: my desire *is* for this to be an interim policy which gets replaced by a project-wide policy via an RFC

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: The experiment is a compromise that offsets strict LLM restrictions with a dedicated route for reviewing and merging LLM-created changes.
claims.quote: this policy proposes very strict LLM restrictions on contributions, which is not a universally favoured position. The experiment exists as a compromise to that: providing a dedicated means through which LLM-created changes can still be reviewed and merged.
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: If the experiment succeeds, will LLM supporters just make it canonical by dropping the experimental wording?
claims.quote: What do pro-LLM people intend to do in this case? Treat the experiment as canonical, remove experimental wording from the policy, and call that a simple wording fix?

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: If others in the project doubt that the accepted LLM contributions are worthwhile, what outcome would be acceptable, and would any data change minds?
claims.quote: What would be an acceptable outcome here? Just tell the people cautious against LLMs that this is the policy, that you're going to refuse to change it, and continue on like this?

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: The experimental framing only works if people agree on what experiment means here and how it can succeed or fail.
claims.quote: I think that the experimental framing only works if people understand what experiment means in this context, and how the experiment is allowed to succeed or fail.

claims.author: joshtriplett
claims.claim: The experiment may produce mixed results that call for stricter rules in some areas and looser ones in others.
claims.quote: I can also imagine the experiment producing more nuanced results that need changes in both directions.

claims.author: joshtriplett
claims.claim: The project already appears to agree firmly that first-party LLM-based security analysis is valuable.
claims.quote: the project seems to have a pretty firm consensus on the value of first-party LLM-based security analysis

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: The most likely result of the experiment is a nuanced discussion and adjustments, while the real worry is outright cancellation or permanent adoption.
claims.quote: I do think that the most likely outcome of the experiment is a nuanced policy discussion and potential changes to the experiment itself.

claims.author: tmandry
claims.claim: The wording calling the experiment non-permanent was added after reviewers had checked their boxes, so it cannot justify the policy's framing.
claims.quote: That wording was added in 356eea010d5bcdf21d4ca57cbdd1e2e6901be455 _after_ the other reviewers had already checked their boxes.

claims.author: tmandry
claims.claim: When 30 people can each block a change, the policy is permanent in practice, not experimental.
claims.quote: In a polarized environment where 30 people can individually block a change, a policy isn't "experimental", it's effectively permanent.

claims.author: tmandry
claims.claim: Calling the policy an experiment is misleading unless there is an easy way to change it.
claims.quote: Without a low-friction way to change the policy, calling it "an experiment only" is a misnomer.

claims.author: tmandry
claims.claim: The circuit breaker makes the project risky and unwelcoming right now for LLM-using contributors, including employees at nearly every major tech company.
claims.quote: The problem with the circuit breaker is that it creates a risky and unwelcoming environment **today** for a class of contributors.

claims.author: tmandry
claims.claim: At many companies AI is standard tooling, and developers often cannot stop using it without harming their careers.
claims.quote: In many cases individuals do not have the choice to stop using it, or doing so would harm their careers.

claims.author: tmandry
claims.claim: Reasonable guardrails on LLM use, as the policy had before, are workable, unlike a cutoff.
claims.quote: Putting reasonable guard rails around that use, as the policy was doing, is workable.

claims.author: tmandry
claims.claim: LLVM shows that sustained corporate contribution is achievable, so company incentives alone do not explain Rust's difficulties.
claims.quote: While I think their performance and promotion structures are partly to blame, it is not the full story. LLVM has managed to do it for years.

claims.author: tmandry
claims.claim: The circuit breaker makes it unacceptably risky to justify starting a Rust compiler team at a company.
claims.quote: That creates an unacceptable risk for anyone trying to justify starting a Rust compiler team at a company.

claims.author: tmandry
claims.claim: Companies would stop investing time and keep patches downstream rather than upstreaming them.
claims.quote: It's that they will stop investing the time in the first place. Nothing requires them to upstream their patches.

claims.author: lumi-me-not
claims.claim: Project restrictions could give employees leverage to stop using generative AI, since their companies have to follow the project's rules.
claims.quote: Wouldn't this just give those employees more leverage to stop using GenAI? The company wants to contribute to a project that does not allow it

claims.author: lumi-me-not
claims.claim: Corporations should not dictate what the project accepts.
claims.quote: I also believe it is dangerous to let corporations dictate what the project should accept or not.

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: Employers forcing staff to use AI is corporate abuse and should not shape Rust's policy.
claims.quote: I don't think that the corporate abuse should dictate Rust's policy.

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: Companies that want to contribute must follow the project's rules, just as they must on respecting people of all backgrounds.
claims.quote: If a company wants to contribute to the project, they have to follow our rules.

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: Arguments for allowing LLMs should at least rest on the technology's merits, not on employees being forced to use it.
claims.quote: Any argument in favour of LLM usage should *at minimum* be on the merits of the technology

claims.author: traviscross
claims.claim: Contributions from companies depend on individuals who argue for them at personal cost, and the policy would make their job harder.
claims.quote: *People* in companies, such as @tmandry, make those contributions happen — at personal cost — by convincing others it's in the enlightened self-interest of the company to do this.

claims.author: traviscross
claims.claim: Tech companies do not need Rust, so the project loses if it deters their contributions.
claims.quote: Tech companies will survive just fine without contributing to Rust.

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: Barriers that companies impose on their employees are not the project's doing, and the project should not give way to them.
claims.quote: We are not making things more difficult for employees; companies are making things more difficult for employees, and we should not yield to companies abusing their employees

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: Being forced to use an LLM is not an argument on the merits for allowing LLM contributions.
claims.quote: But "help, I'm being forced to use this tool against my will" is *obviously* not a discussion on the merits.

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: An experimental policy is by nature not ordinary policy, and the worry is that this framing will be forgotten over time.
claims.quote: an experiment *inherently* has this kind of framing; "experimental" policy is not regular policy in its own, and the worry is that this framing would be lost in the future.

claims.author: clarfonthey
claims.claim: If the goal is indefinite policy, it should be reframed as something other than an experiment.
claims.quote: That is a valid concern to potentially frame this as *not an experiment* if the goal is to keep this as indefinite policy

claims.author: traviscross
claims.claim: Companies that require AI tooling do so legitimately for efficiency, and calling that abuse does not help.
claims.quote: Companies that require employees to use provided AI tooling do so because they believe it makes work more efficient.  Since they're paying those people for work, that's a legitimate thing to do.

claims.author: traviscross
claims.claim: The project chooses freely, and its choices affect who chooses to help it.
claims.quote: We're free to make our own choices.  Nobody is coercing us.  And others are free to make their own choices too, including whether to help us.

claims.author: workingjubilee
claims.claim: The pro-LLM position in this debate has driven away the time and motivation of several contributors.
claims.quote: The perspectives advocated by that position during this entire debate has been a major obstruction to my, and several other contributor's, time and desire to keep working on Rust.

claims.author: workingjubilee
claims.claim: Corporations upstream code partly to shift the risk of its correctness onto the project, while using error-prone tools.
claims.quote: A risk they take on while using tools that are known to have errors and disclaimed to have factual inaccuracies, to boot.

claims.author: workingjubilee
claims.claim: The project should not have to stay open indefinitely to tools whose engineering consequences at scale are still unknown.
claims.quote: It is madness that we are being told that we must be exceedingly and indefinitely hospitable to things for which the engineering consequences of their use at scale have largely not yet been discovered

claims.author: workingjubilee
claims.claim: Rust's value to corporations lies in being different from them, which accommodating their tooling would erode.
claims.quote: What is there left for those corporations to invest *in* if we make ourselves just like them? We have to be *actually different*.

claims.author: phaylon
claims.claim: Organizations that use AI will already have AI-made fixes, so the cost is the extra effort needed to upstream them, not coercion.
claims.quote: So this is less about being forced to use AI for upstream work, and more about how much additional effort they have to spend *after* they have arrived at a solution.

claims.author: phaylon
claims.claim: Developers might have to persuade employers to fund rework, possibly a clean-room rewrite, and then persuade reviewers it is clean.
claims.quote: the developer would have to convince their employer to spend additional resources (potentially even to fully clean room the solution?) and then also convince the project/team members that it is clean enough

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: The circuit breaker only means a contributor may wait up to 10 days, not that they must redo work.
claims.quote: That is not what the policy says, no. The policy says you may have to wait up to 10 days.

claims.author: phaylon
claims.claim: The circuit breaker pushes contributors to deploy locally while they wait, or to write non-AI contributions instead.
claims.quote: So the incentive is already to deploy locally until-we-get-around-to-it. If you don't want that hassle, you'd have to produce a non-AI contribution.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: Running a fork is always easier than upstreaming, so the debate concerns how much review is required, not structural incentives.
claims.quote: there is no way we can make it easier to upstream code than to just run your own fork, other than completely discarding the idea of a review process.

claims.author: jyn514
claims.claim: The circuit-breaker window is there to trigger a discussion and allow the policy to change, not to apply old rules blindly.
claims.quote: which is why the point of the window is to have a *discussion*, not just to blindly follow the rules we made months ago.

claims.author: BoxyUwU
claims.claim: The policy cannot work as a real experiment because people do not believe it can actually be changed.
claims.quote: this policy is getting slightly screwed over by the fact that it can't be a real "experiment" because people (myself included) don't think it'll actually be able to be changed.

claims.author: BoxyUwU
claims.claim: The proposed leadership-council LLM committee would solve the changeability problem and make this PR unnecessary, so this policy should wait for it.
claims.quote: rust-lang/leadership-council#308 seems like a nice way to resolve that and would obviate this PR (and its associated nightmarish billion person FCP).

claims.author: joshtriplett
claims.claim: The committee is about how policy evolves and project-wide policy, which should not hold up a policy for rust-lang/rust.
claims.quote: the goal of the committee is to provide paths for policy evolution/adaptation, and to write policy that will be more broadly applicable across the project, but that shouldn't stop us from enacting policy for `rust-lang/rust` if we can.

claims.author: nnethercote
claims.claim: The policy has met the approval threshold in four teams with 26 approvals, so it should go ahead without further delay.
claims.quote: It has reached the required N-2 approval threshold for four different teams. That is 26 separate approvals, an extraordinary number.

claims.author: BoxyUwU
claims.claim: An expected easier way to update the policy soon, such as the LLM committee, makes accepting it with suboptimal parts more tolerable.
claims.quote: I expect us to find a way to more easily update this policy in the short/medium term, for example the LLM committee proposal (rust-lang/leadership-council#308).

P1.statement: The policy should cover only rust-lang/rust, not subtrees, submodules, dependencies or other repositories.

P2.statement: rust-lang/rust is receiving a flood of low-effort, mostly LLM-written PRs.

P3.statement: Having some policy, even a permissive one, beats no policy, which would bring confusion, distrust and wasted reviewer and moderator time.

P4.statement: The policy deliberately bans more than strictly needed so it is easy to understand and moderate.

P5.statement: A repo-specific policy fits because project-wide agreement is impractical and teams need different standards.

P6.statement: The teams that review rust-lang/rust are entitled to set its policy, which does not commit the wider project, and the Leadership Council is not the right body.

P7.statement: Escalating to the Leadership Council or a project-wide policy would add process and block the policy, as it has blocked earlier ones.

P8.statement: The policy has met its approval threshold and should go ahead without further delay.

P9.statement: The policy effectively commits the whole project and reflects a small opinionated group, so a trusted top-level body like the Leadership Council should decide it.

P10.statement: A Leadership Council-appointed group should gather data and create a permanent policy.

P11.statement: This policy should be explicitly interim, replaced by a project-wide policy or reverted if no replacement emerges.

P12.statement: The policy should wait for the proposed Leadership Council LLM committee, which would solve the changeability problem.

P13.statement: An expected easier update path such as the LLM committee makes accepting the policy with suboptimal parts tolerable.

P14.statement: Looser rules for project members than for newcomers would entrench power and feel unfriendly.

P15.statement: A lenient responsible-use policy ignores reputational harm and makes moderation harder.

P16.statement: The policy needs a time limit, automatic revisit trigger or precise allowed cases so it gets revisited.
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

P17.statement: A threshold-of-originality exception is needed so well-meaning contributors are not forced to discard, rewrite or lie.

P18.statement: There is no consensus for a full ban, which would drive people away, so the policy reflects what is politically possible.

P19.statement: Ethical objections can only be satisfied by a full ban, so a policy addressing practical concerns cannot meet them.

P20.statement: Ruling the main objections out of scope only sets them aside, creating the appearance of consensus; all aspects should be included.

P21.statement: Social and environmental impacts of LLMs should be in scope, and leaving ethics out will alienate people the project has worked to include.

P22.statement: The policy should be adopted as written without ethics, since later policies can fix its shortcomings.

P23.statement: The policy should not be pushed through with a plan to fix objections later, since its rules will be very hard to change.

P24.statement: The FCP should get extra time because the late changes were large.

P25.statement: The policy is balanced and nuanced and does not read as a project stance for or against AI.

P26.statement: The policy can reasonably be read as anti-AI and is not neutral, since banning code writing and merely having it set a precedent.

P27.statement: The policy is so restrictive that it is worse than no policy, setting a precedent that harms potential contributors.

P28.statement: US lawyers initially indicate LLM output likely poses no copyright problem.

P29.statement: Private feedback suggests no silent majority opposes the policy, though the sample is unrepresentative.

P30.statement: Maintainers should have flexibility to judge AI-assisted PRs by quality, with guidelines rather than hard rules that cause fairness disputes.

P31.statement: Treating an honestly disclosed AI-generated PR as an instant code-of-conduct violation is untenable.

P32.statement: Low-autonomy AI uses are largely solved in practice while end-to-end AI work is risky.

P33.statement: The line should be drawn by the AI's detectable level of autonomy rather than creation versus review.

P34.statement: AI is poor at code review because models are too agreeable.

P35.statement: Once a restrictive policy is in place, its supporters will have no incentive to compromise.

P36.statement: The policy will be very hard to change because many people can each block any change.

P37.statement: Calling the policy an experiment is misleading because people do not believe it can easily be changed.

P38.statement: The compromise provisions will be effectively permanent regardless of their experimental label.
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

P39.statement: The experiment lacks defined parameters, success criteria or an end, leaving people disagreeing over whether it is temporary.

P40.statement: The policy text says the experiment exists to inform future policy and is not meant to be permanent.

P41.statement: The non-permanence wording was added after reviewers approved, so it cannot justify the policy's framing.

P42.statement: Ending the experiment after a fixed time or PR count would not work because no default outcome forces negotiation.

P43.statement: The 50% circuit breaker would not bring both sides back to negotiate and could deepen polarization.

P44.statement: The circuit breaker sets a boundary no side wants, forcing a discussion and review of the policy.

P45.statement: If LLMs are used in over half of PRs the arrangement is no longer an experiment, justifying a circuit breaker.

P46.statement: A circuit breaker capping LLM PRs at half of merged PRs should be added.

P47.statement: The policy must prevent pushing non-LLM contributors out, which the pro-LLM side has already been doing.

P48.statement: Halting a category of PRs at an arbitrary limit is an unjustified last-minute change that enforces an aesthetic limit rather than reducing harm.

P49.statement: The circuit breaker is excessive control that marks LLM-using contributors as second-class.

P50.statement: Reasonable guardrails on LLM use are workable, unlike a cutoff.

P51.statement: The circuit breaker deters corporate contributors and investment, pushing patches downstream, and the project loses by deterring them.

P52.statement: AI tooling is standard and legitimately required at many companies, so developers cannot easily stop using it.

P53.statement: Corporations should not dictate what the project accepts; they must follow its rules.

P54.statement: Employers forcing staff to use AI is abuse and should not shape Rust's policy.

P55.statement: Being forced to use LLMs by employers is not an argument on the merits for allowing them.

P56.statement: Project restrictions could give employees leverage to avoid generative AI.

P57.statement: LLVM shows sustained corporate contribution is achievable, so company incentives alone do not explain Rust's difficulties.

P58.statement: Corporations upstream code partly to shift correctness risk onto the project while using error-prone tools.

P59.statement: The project need not stay open indefinitely to tools whose engineering consequences at scale are unknown.

P60.statement: Rust's value to corporations lies in being different from them, which accommodating their tooling would erode.

P61.statement: The breaker's cost is the effort to rework or clean-room AI-made fixes before upstreaming them.

P62.statement: The circuit breaker only means a contributor may wait up to 10 days, not redo work.

P63.statement: The circuit breaker pushes contributors to deploy locally while waiting or write non-AI contributions instead.

P64.statement: Running a fork is always easier than upstreaming, so the debate is about how much review is required.

P65.statement: A policy banning AI would attract contributors who prefer software built without AI, as lists of such projects show.

P66.statement: Banning LLMs would drive away contributors who value moderate LLM use.

P67.statement: Policy should not be decided based on outside lists that shame projects.

P68.statement: The No-AI list promotes projects and is not a harassment tool.

P69.statement: The compromise is acceptable because the main concern is AI authoring contributions, not review or lookup.

P70.statement: Clearly marked, vetted AI-generated reports should be allowed as supplemental material so security work is not impeded.

P71.statement: If AI-found security issues flood in, an exemption can be requested later.

P72.statement: The project already agrees first-party LLM-based security analysis is valuable.

P73.statement: An alternative set of guidelines for allowing LLM-authored code has been drafted.
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

P74.statement: A wide range of policies would be acceptable apart from extremes.

P75.statement: Handling LLM contributions case by case would be fine because there are currently few of them; no policy should be considered.

P76.statement: Many LLM-related contributions are not slop and come from newcomers, making case-by-case handling hard.

P77.statement: Does the policy require even experienced developers to use the experimental process for LLM-generated content?
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

P78.statement: LLM-generated code is unreliable and hallucinates, so a full ban is better for a compiler valued for safety.

P79.statement: Humans cannot reliably catch machine-generated errors, especially as LLMs erode their skill and judgement.

P80.statement: LLMs cause deskilling and shift skills to a few corporations.

P81.statement: Even limited permission for LLM code is too much and a ban is needed.

P82.statement: Rust would be better off ending than relying on LLMs that undermine its safety goals.

P83.statement: Would opponents prefer no Rust project or no policy over one that uses LLMs?

P84.statement: Rust thrived before LLMs, so it is a false dichotomy that a full ban would threaten the project.

P85.statement: Seeking consensus should not override what is right, so a ban should not wait for consensus.

P86.statement: The policy authors are trusted to merge rustc code, so they can be trusted to allow LLMs safely.

P87.statement: A person certifying safety-critical rustc builds believes the policy will not hurt reliability.

P88.statement: Trusting maintainers' judgement on code does not mean trusting their judgement on LLM policy.

P89.statement: The added experimental-use section resolves the revisit concern even without automatic expiry.
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

P90.statement: Requiring authors to find a reviewer first is not ideal but necessary given limited review capacity.
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

P91.statement: The soundness-critical restriction relies on reviewer discretion but its guidelines and early discussion help.
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

P92.statement: The policy is a cautious compromise: it defaults to no while offering a dedicated route for reviewed LLM changes.
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

P93.statement: The policy's complex rules signal low trust in fellow reviewers.
about: allow only by prior arrangement with reviewers

P94.statement: A group should experiment with handling LLM content instead of over-specifying review details.

P95.statement: The social friction around LLMs will cost the community more than LLM code is worth.

P96.statement: Compiler-team decisions shape Rust's wider culture and should not be judged in isolation.

P97.statement: Experienced facilitators should be brought in because the conflict is a social problem.

P98.statement: Project members decide while outside input is heard but not decisive.

P99.statement: The project currently has almost no LLM restrictions and this policy adds significant ones.

P100.statement: The policy is a welcome step in the right direction.

P101.statement: The real dangers are an internal split and maintainer burnout from slop PRs, making some policy necessary.

P102.statement: LLMs should be barred from meetings unless members consent.

P103.statement: A meetings rule is out of scope for a code-contribution policy and will be reverted.

P104.statement: The policy should state that LLMs are optional and never required for contributing.

P105.statement: If the experiment succeeds, will LLM supporters make it canonical by dropping the experimental wording?

P106.statement: What outcome or data would change minds about whether accepted LLM contributions are worthwhile?

P107.statement: The experiment will most likely yield mixed results and nuanced adjustments rather than cancellation or permanent adoption.

P108.statement: The policy is long but its nuance is needed now and it can be summarized after merging.

edges.why: Argues a policy beats the confusion of case-by-case handling.
Argues any policy beats having none.
Says case-by-case handling is hard because many LLM PRs are not slop.
Says LLM-involved contributions are currently few, against a flood.
A flood of slop PRs motivates having a policy.
Burnout from slop PRs makes some policy necessary.
Prefers reviewer flexibility over deliberately broad hard rules.
Argues for an exception to the broad ban.
Objects to treating disclosed AI use as a violation.

cruxes.question: Can LLM-authored code be reviewed and merged into the compiler without unacceptable risk to correctness and reliability?

sides.answer: No; LLM code is too unreliable and human review cannot reliably catch its errors, so any allowance is too much
Yes, under constraints such as reviewer pre-arrangement, low autonomy and soundness limits

cruxes.why_decisive: Most arguments for a full ban versus the gated experiment rest on whether reviewed LLM code is safe enough; settling it removes the core technical dispute.
cruxes.settles_by: Empirical evidence: defect, revert and review-effort data on LLM-assisted PRs merged under the policy versus comparable human PRs.

cruxes.question: Will the experimental allowance actually be revisable, or will it be permanent in practice?

sides.answer: Permanent in practice: changes need near-unanimous approval and the label lacks an end or criteria
Revisable: the text says it is non-permanent, and review and adjustment are expected or easier paths are coming

cruxes.why_decisive: Both the pro-ban side's fear of entrenchment and the demand for sunset clauses, interim status or a circuit breaker flow from this question.
cruxes.settles_by: Governance design and track record: the actual change procedure, whether a sunset or success criteria are added, and whether the planned committee materializes.

cruxes.question: Should ethical, social and environmental objections to LLMs be within the scope of this policy?

sides.answer: Yes; excluding them sets them aside, manufactures consensus and alienates people
No; the policy should address practical concerns like quality and burden, and ethics cannot be met short of a ban anyway

cruxes.why_decisive: The scope ruling determines whether the ban case is even admissible and whether the current consensus is seen as legitimate.
cruxes.settles_by: Normative judgement about the project's values and precedents for ethical commitments in its other policies.

cruxes.question: Does adoption require consensus, and does the lack of consensus for a full ban settle the matter?

sides.answer: Yes; a community project can only pass policy by consensus, so the policy reflects what is politically possible
No; consensus should not override what is right, and apparent consensus is an artifact of excluded arguments

cruxes.why_decisive: If consensus is binding, the full-ban position cannot prevail and the debate reduces to tuning the compromise.
cruxes.settles_by: Governance judgement about the project's decision rules (FCP, consensus norms).

cruxes.question: Who has authority to set this policy: the teams reviewing rust-lang/rust, or a project-wide body such as the Leadership Council?

sides.answer: The reviewing teams, scoped to the repo, without escalation
A project-wide body, because the policy effectively commits the whole project

cruxes.why_decisive: The procedural objections, calls to delay, and proposals for interim status all hinge on which body is legitimate.
cruxes.settles_by: The project's governance charter and judgement on whether the repo policy de facto binds the project.

cruxes.question: Is a hard cap on the share of LLM PRs (the circuit breaker) justified given its effect on corporate and LLM-using contributors?

sides.answer: Justified: it protects non-LLM contributors, keeps the experiment bounded, and corporations must follow project rules
Unjustified: it is arbitrary, marks LLM users as second-class, deters corporate investment and will not bring sides back to the table

cruxes.why_decisive: The circuit breaker was a late change that reopened the corporate, welcome and changeability disputes; its fate largely determines whether the compromise holds.
cruxes.settles_by: Data on contributor composition and corporate contribution behavior, plus judgement on what the experiment's boundary should be.

cruxes.question: Is the volume of LLM contributions large enough that a formal policy is better than reviewer discretion?

sides.answer: Yes; there is a flood of slop and no policy brings confusion and burnout
No; LLM contributions are few and quality-based reviewer judgement suffices, or the policy is worse than none

cruxes.why_decisive: It decides whether any policy is needed at all, framing every other question.
cruxes.settles_by: Counts of LLM-involved PRs and moderator and reviewer time spent on them.
